title: Preseason ACL Screening for Girls' Clubs
one_liner: A 10-second phone-video landing screen at tryouts that flags risky mechanics and routes athletes to prevention programs and PT.
customer: Youth club directors and high school athletic directors (pay $8-15 per athlete); PT and sports-medicine clinics (pay for referred athletes and return-to-sport testing).
problem: Chain: women's pro leagues drive rapid growth of girls' club sports, more year-round load raises ACL tears (girls' rates are several times boys'), and PT and orthopedic capacity is short (outpatient PT vacancy rates around 17 percent, Medicare pressure pushing clinics to cash-pay), while return-to-sport decisions still rely on subjective checks. Nobody screens 400,000 girls before the season.
solution: Phone or existing AI-camera footage of a drop jump and single-leg landing, analyzed by markerless pose estimation; flagged athletes get a tailored FIFA-11+-style program by SMS video and a 4-week re-test; PT partners pay for return-to-sport test packages using the same tech. Framed as movement-quality coaching with measurable pre/post improvement, not injury prediction.
why_now: Open-source markerless biomechanics is now good enough for field use, AI cameras are already in clubs (roughly $949 plus subscription), and cash-pay PT clinics need a top-of-funnel; parents already spend thousands per year on club sports.
revenue_model: $8-15 per athlete billed to the club or added at registration; $1.5-3k per year per PT clinic partner; $49 per return-to-sport test.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is the club (liability and differentiation), and the PT clinic pays for demand. Screens are weak predictors, so a small validation study and honest positioning as an intervention-adherence tool is the moat.
first_30_days: Partner with two clubs at tryouts (about 200 athletes), a sports PT clinic and a university biomechanist to validate against reference measures, produce a one-page athlete report, and take a $500 sponsorship from the clinic.

title: Transformer Buying Co-op for Small Utilities
one_liner: Pool the orders of hundreds of rural co-ops and municipal utilities into one standardized spec so they can get in line together.
customer: Roughly 900 electric distribution co-ops and 2,000 municipal utilities, plus solar and storage developers. They pay a procurement fee.
problem: Power transformer lead times average 128 weeks, distribution transformer prices are up as much as 95%, and over 40M units are past service life. Small utilities order in dozens with bespoke specs and go to the back of the line. One contrarian says standardized units can ship in 12-14 months, so procurement, not manufacturing, is the bottleneck.
solution: Pre-negotiated framework agreements with two or three manufacturers (including offshore) for a small menu of standard units, for example pad-mount 25-167 kVA and 5-10 MVA substation units. Add a predictive replacement list built from age and AMI loading data, a financed rotating stock pool, and slot reassignment among members.
why_now: Data centers outbid utilities for manufacturing slots, lead times are at 128 weeks, and co-ops and munis are scrambling with no purchasing leverage.
revenue_model: 2-4% procurement fee, a stock-pool financing and storage spread, and $10-30k a year SaaS for replacement planning.
non_obvious_insight: Part of the shortage is fragmentation. Manufacturers prioritize buyers who commit to standard specs and volume, and small utilities are collectively huge but individually invisible.
first_30_days: Collect 30 co-op and muni transformer spec sheets. Propose a common spec at a state co-op association or APPA event. Get five utilities to sign LOIs for a 200-unit pilot order. Talk to two mid-size manufacturers with open 2028 slots.

title: Grant Recovery Desk for Small Cities
one_liner: A contingency-fee grant compliance and reimbursement service for small cities receiving FEMA, DOJ and counter-drone money with no staff to document it.
customer: Towns and counties with populations of 5-100K, especially those receiving disaster reimbursements and new safety grants (for example the $500M FEMA counter-UAS program).
problem: Small governments lose federal reimbursements to incomplete documentation, procurement missteps and audit findings. With federal agencies shrinking and reorganizations stalled in court, help is thinner. Dallas County is cutting IT staff, and local budgets are tight.
solution: A software-plus-service program that structures the grant lifecycle: eligibility check, procurement compliance, receipt capture, quarterly reporting and closeout audit packages. It uses AI to read award terms and flag non-compliant purchases before they happen. Paid from recovered funds.
why_now: New grant streams (counter-drone, cyber, disaster) are landing at localities while federal grant-management staff are being cut. Regulators enforce documentation harder as budgets tighten.
revenue_model: Contingency of 4-8% of recovered or protected award dollars, with a minimum retainer. A city with $2M in awards yields about $80-160K.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer pays nothing up front, and the alternative is losing money already awarded. Contingency pricing turns a dreaded compliance cost into free money for a small clerk's office.
first_30_days: Offer free award-file reviews to 10 small cities identified from public award lists. Build a compliance checklist per program. Sign 2 contingency deals.

title: Ceiling-Camera Auto-Logging for Strength Gyms
one_liner: Cameras that watch the lifting floor and automatically log every athlete's sets, reps, load and bar speed with no phone.
customer: Independent strength gyms, CrossFit boxes, powerlifting clubs and high school and college weight rooms paying $199-499 per month.
problem: Progress tracking is the strongest retention lever in lifting, but manual logging is tedious so most members skip it, and coaches at high athlete ratios cannot see everyone's sets or spot stalls.
solution: Two to four ceiling cameras plus an edge box; vision models recognize the exercise, plate colors (load), rep count and bar velocity; lifters are identified by wristband or QR rather than faces; a coach dashboard flags stalls, form drift and missed sessions and a member app fills logs automatically.
why_now: 2025-26 vision foundation models handle exercise and object recognition at the edge on cheap hardware, and tightening biometric privacy laws push products toward non-facial identification.
revenue_model: $199-499 per gym per month plus $1.5-3k install; school weight-room licenses; velocity-based-training analytics as an add-on.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is the coach or owner, not the member: automatic logging gives coaches visibility that drives retention and coaching upsells, a Hudl for the weight room. Avoiding face recognition sidesteps biometric-law exposure.
first_30_days: Install DIY hardware (about $800) in two friendly gyms, label two weeks of squat, bench and deadlift footage with plate detection, offer a free three-month pilot, and measure log completion and member retention to justify $299 per month.

title: Kin Circles: Chosen-Family Covenants for Solo Agers
one_liner: A structured program where 6-8 unrelated adults form a witnessed, legally backed chosen-family circle that covers emergencies, hospital discharge and funerals.
customer: Adults aged 50-75 with no spouse or children (AARP finds about 12% of Americans over 50 age solo, and Census data show 15.2 million adults over 55 are childless), with senior-living operators and hospitals as second-tier buyers.
problem: At crisis moments such as surgery, discharge, dementia and death, solo agers have no designated person who is legally empowered and emotionally committed to show up. Friendships drift because obligations are unspecified, unwitnessed and not legally recognised.
solution: A six-week guided formation of a Kin Circle of 6-8 people. It produces a written covenant of specific mutual obligations (rides after surgery, weekly check-ins, holiday dinners), a legal packet through flat-fee partner attorneys (health-care proxy, HIPAA release, power of attorney, funeral instructions), and a public vow ceremony with witnesses. An annual renewal ritual and a simple escalation ladder (if someone misses two check-ins the circle is pinged) keep it alive.
why_now: Solo aging is a demographic wave: 43% of women aged 75+ live alone, and about 4 in 10 childless older adults live alone. Loneliness is a public-health issue, and 'chosen family' is mainstream. Guardianship abuse headlines have made older adults want plans that keep them out of the court system.
revenue_model: Formation packages of roughly $500-800 per person, membership of about $12 per month, annual renewal rituals at around $150 per circle, and licensing of the program to senior-living operators and hospital discharge teams. Legal work is sold by the attorney at a flat fee, with no fee-splitting.
non_obvious_insight: Marriage works because it bundles vow, witnesses and legal status into an obligation stack, and platonic groups lack all three. Unbundle that stack and rebuild it for a group; six to eight people share the load so no one burns out, unlike a single friend or a single adult child.
first_30_days: Recruit three pilot circles through community centers, Meetup and solo-aging forums. Sign two estate-planning attorneys for a flat-fee legal packet. Host the first witnessed 'vow night' and film it for testimonials.

title: Weather Forecasts for GPS Jamming
one_liner: A crowd-sensed, forecastable map of GNSS jamming and spoofing for the civil operators nobody warns: survey and RTK fleets, drone operators and marine underwriters.
customer: First: commercial drone operators, RTK survey and construction machine-control fleets, and precision-ag contractors in the Baltics, Poland, Finland, Turkey and the Gulf, at $99 to $499 a month. Second: marine war-risk MGAs, P&I clubs and route planners, at $50k to $250k a year.
problem: Jamming and spoofing have surged (EASA revised its GNSS-interference bulletin again in July 2026; Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb dominate ship incidents; insurers are bracing for mega-claims). Operators learn about it when a drone flies away or autosteer fails. Public maps such as GPSJam are daily averages built from ADS-B, too coarse for a specific field or route hour.
solution: A sensor network of cheap multi-band GNSS receivers and opted-in Android raw-GNSS phones (hosts are farmers, truckers and drone pilots, paid in free forecasts). It detects carrier-to-noise collapse and spoofing signatures at about 1 km resolution in near real time. On top of that sits a forecast (jammers repeat by hour and geometry) and an API/SMS alert such as 'L1 degraded within 20 km of your flight plan 14:00-16:00'. A signed position-integrity report is offered to insurers.
why_now: Dual-frequency GNSS chips cost about $10 and expose raw measurements. Android exposes raw GNSS data. Jamming intensity rose sharply through 2025-26, and insurers and P&I clubs have started buying authentication tech, so the demand signal is visible in the market.
revenue_model: SaaS of $99 to $999 a month for fleets. Annual data licences of $50k to $250k to insurers and MGAs. Per-report fee for integrity certificates. Optional hardware host kit sold at cost.
non_obvious_insight: Jamming is spatially and temporally patterned like weather, so it can be forecast, not just mapped afterward. The paying buyers are not militaries but civil operators whose exposure nobody prices. The sensor network gets built for free if you pay hosts in forecasts.
first_30_days: Deploy 30 receivers with three agri-drone and survey firms in Poland and the Baltics. Email a weekly jamming map overlaid on their own flight logs. Sign 10 paying users at 99 EUR a month. Send a route-level sample dataset to two marine war-risk underwriters.

title: A Price Index and Exchange for Agent Labor
one_liner: Publish the going rate and accuracy for standardized agent-delivered tasks (per 1,000 invoices, per verified ticket resolution), then let buyers run reverse auctions against it.
customer: CFOs, procurement and ops leaders at enterprises buying agent services, investors and analysts, and later the agent vendors that bid for work.
problem: Buyers have no reference price. Vendor pricing is opaque and shifting from seats to outcomes, quality varies widely, and Gartner says only about 130 of thousands of 'agentic' vendors are real. Unit token prices fell about 67% but bills rose, so nobody knows what a task should cost.
solution: Define standardized task classes with public test sets and acceptance criteria (invoice extraction and coding, tier-1 support resolution, KYC document review, meeting scheduling). Run blinded monthly bake-offs across vendors on hidden holdouts and publish a quality and cost-per-verified-outcome index. Sell buyer-side bake-offs on customers' own data. Later add an RFQ exchange with escrow released when acceptance tests pass.
why_now: Outcome pricing arrived in 2026, agent-washing is rampant, and benchmarks exist for models but not end-to-end vendors. Project Vend-style real-world evaluations show that outcomes need checklists and supervision to be trustworthy.
revenue_model: $20-$60k/year subscriptions for enterprises and investors, $15-$40k custom bake-offs, and a 3-5% exchange take rate later.
non_obvious_insight: Markets need a benchmark price before they need a marketplace, as freight and housing indices came first. Agent labor has large quality and price dispersion, and the party that publishes the reference sets the negotiation frame for the whole category.
first_30_days: Pick 2 task classes and assemble public plus holdout data. Run 6 vendors and publish the first index free with full methodology. Sell the first custom bake-off to a buyer and use it as a case study.

title: GLP-1 Stipend-in-a-Box for Small Employers
one_liner: A counsel-reviewed HRA wrapper that lets small employers subsidize $149-$299 cash-pay GLP-1s with a capped monthly stipend.
customer: Employers with roughly 10-200 employees, sold through brokers, PEOs and HRA administrators.
problem: Large-employer coverage fell from 72% to 60% and more are dropping, while 27% of employers already point staff to LillyDirect or NovoCare. Direct-to-employer vendors like Waltz Health and 9amHealth target mid and large plans. Small employers can't carve out of a fully insured plan, and stipend plans raise ERISA, ACA and tax questions they can't answer.
solution: A packaged structure (QSEHRA, ICHRA or limited-purpose HRA, depending on group size) with plan documents, capped stipend rules, receipt-based reimbursement from DTC pharmacies, minimum-essential-coverage checks, and optional coaching. Brokers get a commission.
why_now: $149-$299 manufacturer cash prices make a capped stipend cheaper than open-ended coverage. Employers just dropped or plan to drop coverage before open enrollment, and TrumpRx and DTC channels launched in 2026.
revenue_model: $5-8 per employee per month plus ~5% of stipend flow, with broker commission share.
non_obvious_insight: The fight is over who administers the wrapper for the 90% of employers that PBM carve-out vendors don't serve. Compliance and broker distribution matter more than the coaching content.
first_30_days: Have an ERISA attorney draft the plan documents. Partner with an existing QSEHRA or HRA administrator. Pilot with 10 small employers (~300 lives) through two brokers and measure uptake and cost per participant.

title: Entry-Integrity Layer for Contests and Festivals
one_liner: Intake screening and a finalist verification desk for photo, film, screenplay and art open calls that fear an AI-winner scandal.
customer: Organizers of photo contests, film festivals, screenwriting and comics competitions, and art open calls, especially those that already collect entry fees through FilmFreeway, Submittable or their own forms.
problem: Generative tools make entries free to produce, so organizers face reviewer overload and reputational risk from an AI-made winner. Platform stigma around AI content has just hardened (TIDAL, Snap, Spotify, YouTube all acted between May and Aug 2026), so a scandal now costs more. Organizers verify nothing beyond a checkbox.
solution: A plugin or service that (1) screens each entry on intake with C2PA and SynthID checks, metadata analysis and a detector ensemble, sorting entries into green, amber and red for screeners, (2) asks finalists for a proof pack (raw files, project files or a behind-the-scenes clip), and (3) runs a 48-hour human-reviewed finalist verification that yields a 'Verified Human-Made Finalist' certificate for the winners' announcement. High-volume calls can add a refundable deposit.
why_now: Provenance signals are now common in cameras and tools, detector prices have fallen, and AI-content policies are stricter across platforms, so organizers finally have something to check against and something to lose.
revenue_model: $0.50-2 per-entry surcharge or $500-5,000 per contest, plus $20-60 per verified finalist, renewing annually.
non_obvious_insight: Organizers already charge entry fees, so a $1 integrity fee is invisible to entrants. Only the top 1-3% of entries need deep verification, and the real buyer motive is insurance against one embarrassing scandal.
first_30_days: List 50 mid-size contests with deadlines in Q4-Q1 from FilmFreeway and photo-contest calendars. Offer free finalist verification to the first five in exchange for a case study, run it as a concierge service with tools behind it, then charge $1,500 flat.

title: Pharmacy Friendly Calls, Paid by Adherence Stars
one_liner: Independent pharmacies run weekly human-led friendship calls to isolated refill customers, funded by the Medicare adherence performance that loneliness quietly erodes.
customer: Independent community pharmacies (roughly 18,000 in the US) paying $500-1,200 a month per store, later reimbursed through Medicare Advantage and Part D plan performance and MTM contracts.
problem: Isolated older adults skip refills. Adherence measures for diabetes, RAS-antagonist and statin drugs carry triple weight in Medicare Star ratings, so plans pay for every point. Older adults distrust AI companions (Pew, Jun 2026: 40-46% of 65+ are 'unsure' whether chatbots help or hurt), and startup elder-companion services lack a trusted local face. The corner pharmacist has that trust and a list of exactly who is isolated.
solution: A 'Pharmacy Pal' program. Each store enrolls 40-80 living-alone or homebound refill customers. A paid part-time caller (a retiree or pharmacy tech) makes a weekly 10-minute call using an AI-prepared brief (last call notes, refill gaps, birthdays), and also does a twice-monthly delivery run. Software covers rosters, call briefs, refill-gap alerts and a proportion-of-days-covered dashboard the pharmacy can show plans. The AI never talks to the patient.
why_now: Chain-store closures (Rite Aid's 2025 wind-down among them) made independents the last local pharmacy for many seniors. Plans are squeezed on Star bonuses and margins and want cheap, measurable adherence levers. Pew's 2026 data show older adults distrust chatbots, which reopens the case for human-led programs.
revenue_model: $12-18 per enrolled patient per month, paid by the pharmacy out of retained refills, delivery fees and plan MTM or performance-network payments. Phase two is direct plan contracts priced on measured adherence lift.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders look for an elder-companion buyer among families and social-service agencies. The real loneliness budget for older adults sits inside Star-rating adherence economics, and the trusted delivery channel is the local pharmacist, not an app.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 independent pharmacies through state pharmacist associations and PSAO newsletters. Each pulls 40 patients from refill-gap reports. Run the calls manually with a spreadsheet and an LLM-generated brief. Measure adherence lift against matched non-enrolled patients over 90 days. Charge $500 a month per store from the start.

title: Alt-Data From AI-Training Gig Workers
one_liner: A worker-owned pay-transparency panel for expert data contractors. Its aggregated signals on which domains are hiring, what they pay and how many hours exist become a leading-indicator dataset for investors and rival platforms.
customer: Hedge funds, VCs and AI-lab competitive-intelligence teams pay $30-150k a year for the index. Workers get the basic tier free or for $9-15 a month.
problem: Mercor's reported gross run rate went from about $0.5B to $2B in nine months, and the category claims millions of contractors, yet nobody outside the labs can see which skills are in demand or when a domain saturates. Workers complain of falling pay and have no rate data, while investors price a $10-25B category on anecdotes.
solution: A browser extension plus web app where contractors log, or auto-capture from their own dashboards, pay rate, hours offered, rejections and coarse project category (never confidential content). There is a public 'Levels.fyi for AI gigs' leaderboard by platform and domain, and a paid weekly index of hours availability and pay by domain, with saturation early-warnings.
why_now: The human-data market went from niche to multi-billion in a year, contractors are publicly vocal (HN, Verge, Wired coverage) and investor appetite for AI-adjacent labor data is high. No panel exists.
revenue_model: Institutional data subscriptions ($50-150k a year), a premium worker tier ($9-15 a month) and possibly sponsored placements from challenger platforms recruiting supply.
non_obvious_insight: Gig workers are usually treated as supply, but here they are a sensor network that reads the frontier labs' priorities weeks before any press release. Workers will join because it helps them negotiate and avoid saturated domains. Platforms can't easily object to workers sharing their own pay data, provided the design avoids NDA-covered project details.
first_30_days: Seed 300 members from data-annotation subreddits and Discords with a pay-rate survey. Publish a 'State of expert AI gig pay' report. Pitch 10 funds and 3 VC platform teams a sample weekly index, and land one paid pilot.

title: Frozen Models: Long-Term Support for AI Deployments
one_liner: A 'Red Hat for AI models': host specific model versions with a written 5-7 year availability guarantee, reproducibility pack and migration diff-testing, for companies that cannot let their AI change under them.
customer: Model-risk, compliance and QA leads at mid-size banks, insurers, health-tech and pharma-adjacent firms, and legal-tech teams that have validated an AI workflow. Later, AI-companion products and their users, who care about persona continuity.
problem: Frontier labs retire models on 12-18 month cycles. Every retirement forces re-running evals, re-validating prompts and re-documenting for auditors. When OpenAI retired GPT-4o from ChatGPT on Feb 13, 2026, it set off the #Keep4o backlash, proving people and firms treat model behavior as something they depend on.
solution: Pin and host frozen snapshots of open-weight models (and customers' own fine-tunes), with contractual availability through a stated year, a fixed and documented inference stack (versions, quantization, seeds), and a change-control pack (model card, eval suite, audit logs). Add a migration service that replays your real traffic through old and new models and produces a behavior-diff report when you choose to upgrade.
why_now: Deprecation cycles have shortened and the 2026 GPT-4o episode made instability visible outside engineering teams. Regulators and auditors increasingly ask for documented change control on AI systems, and open-weight models are now good enough for many bounded enterprise tasks. Nobody is selling stability itself as the product.
revenue_model: Monthly hosting subscription plus per-token usage, one-time change-control pack fees, and per-migration diff-testing engagements.
non_obvious_insight: Enterprises don't buy the best model, they buy the model that won't change. Each frontier release is a validation event for regulated buyers, so a vendor whose product is boring stability (like Ubuntu LTS or RHEL) has a natural niche, and the cost side is cheap because old open weights run on modest GPUs. The consumer angle (keeping a beloved persona alive) adds emotional stickiness that pure infra players can't match.
first_30_days: Interview 20 model-risk and compliance leads in banks and insurers. Publish a one-page 'frozen model SLA' with pricing. Host three open-weight snapshots on rented GPUs with a documented inference stack. Close two design partners at $2-5k/month and produce the first reproducibility pack.

title: Old Job Kits for Dementia Sundown Hours
one_liner: A monthly subscription of dignified, occupation-matched 'work' boxes, such as a retired bookkeeper's ledger and receipts or a retired mechanic's hardware bench, that calm sundowning better than puzzles or toys. Aides earn referral commissions.
customer: Adult children caring for a parent with moderate dementia at home (about $34-44 per month), plus adult day programs and memory care activity directors who buy in bulk. The family pays.
problem: From 4 to 7pm many dementia patients get restless, pace and get aggressive. Families use the TV, memory games or, worse, sedatives. Toys and puzzles marketed to dementia patients often insult them; they toss the plush or refuse the coloring book. What actually calms most patients is purposeful work related to the life they used to have: the retired accountant sorting receipts, the teacher grading papers, the seamstress matching buttons, the waiter folding napkins, the farmer sorting seeds.
solution: Family fills out a 3-minute 'what did they do for work?' intake. Each month a box ships with real, adult-looking, safe materials for that career. Examples are a bookkeeper's ledger, adding-machine paper, a rubber stamp and pre-sorted stacks. A teacher gets a stack of old spelling tests with a red pen and gold stars. A mechanic gets large washers and nuts on a workbench tray. Nothing sharp, small or childlike. A card gives the aide or family a 30-second 'handoff line' ('the boss needs these sorted before five'). Aides get a personal referral code and 20 percent commission.
why_now: CMS's push to reduce antipsychotic use in dementia and its GUIDE dementia care model (live since July 2024, with caregiver education and respite requirements) push practices toward cheap non-drug behavior tools. Short-form video is a free channel, since a grandfather 'clocking in' to sort receipts is deeply shareable. Families are stretched by cuts to home care hours and turn to anything that buys them a calm evening.
revenue_model: $34-44 per month subscription with quarterly rotation. Bulk B2B orders of $250 per month per adult day or memory care program. 20 percent referral commissions to aides and care managers. Upsell to 'career library' add-ons and licensed professional-uniform accessories.
non_obvious_insight: The trick is not stimulation but purpose, and it must look like a real job, because anything that looks like a child's toy is rejected as an insult. Also, families ask their aide what to buy, and aides are the most trusted product recommenders in the house, yet no brand has ever paid them. Paying aides a commission creates a distribution channel no ad budget can match and quietly raises their income.
first_30_days: Build 6 career kits (bookkeeper, teacher, mechanic, seamstress, waiter, nurse) for under $18 each from restaurant-supply, office and hardware stores. Film 15 TikTok and Instagram clips with permission from families. Post in three large caregiver Facebook groups and offer 30 free kits in exchange for video testimonials. Give 20 aides referral codes. Sign up 3 local adult day centers for a $250 monthly pilot. Aim for 50 paying subscribers by day 60.

title: Owner-Side Ordering: The Royalty Asymmetry Calculator
one_liner: An advice-only LINE tool that tells franchise convenience-store owners how many fresh items to order and when to mark them down, using the owner's own payoff instead of HQ's.
customer: Franchise convenience-store owners in Japan, especially the many multi-store owners (roughly 55,000 stores nationally, all three chains). They pay a monthly fee plus a share of the waste they cut. First targets are Osaka owners reachable through the franchisee union and owner LINE groups.
problem: The royalty is charged on gross profit calculated as if discarded food never existed. At Seven, HQ absorbs only 15% of disposal cost and the owner absorbs 85%. So HQ's ordering AI and the field counselors (OFC) push order quantities toward what maximizes HQ's royalty, not the owner's take-home. Take a rice ball that costs ¥100 and sells at ¥160. With a 60% royalty on the ¥60 gross profit, the owner keeps about ¥24 when it sells and loses about ¥85 when it is binned. HQ makes about ¥36 on a sale and loses about ¥15 on a discard. The owner-optimal stocking level is far lower than HQ's, and no owner has a tool that shows this. Markdowns would close much of the gap, but staff are reluctant to apply stickers and owners fear the OFC's disapproval.
solution: The owner photographs the daily disposal-scan printout and the hourly sales sheet, or forwards a CSV. The tool never touches HQ systems. Each afternoon it returns a per-category order guide such as 'cut salmon onigiri by 4 at the 16:00 delivery, add 2 tempura udon'. It also gives a markdown clock, for example 'sticker at 20:40, deeper cut at 23:10', calculated from the owner's actual royalty tier, disposal share and sell-through curve. A one-page 'why I ordered less' printout gives the owner data to answer the OFC. Phase two adds an owner-side dashboard showing true hourly wage after royalty and self-labor. It also adds a contract-exit and renegotiation calculator, and anonymized peer benchmarks that owners can use collectively.
why_now: Osaka's minimum wage rises to ¥1,231 on 1 October 2026, up ¥54 after ¥63 last year. Labor is the biggest cost, and waste is the last controllable line item. HQ-side AI ordering is now the default, so owners increasingly follow machine suggestions they cannot audit. Chains have grudgingly allowed markdowns since the JFTC's 2009 order against Seven-Eleven Japan for obstructing them, but owners still lack tools to price them properly.
revenue_model: ¥4,900 per store per month, plus 20-25% of documented waste reduction for the first 12 months. If a store saves ¥80-100k a month, the fee is easy to justify. Multi-store owners get a bundle. Later revenue comes from an owner-benchmark subscription and referrals to specialist franchise lawyers and accountants.
non_obvious_insight: Waste is not a shared problem between HQ and owner. The contract makes it the owner's problem alone, while HQ's revenue is almost indifferent to it. The newsvendor critical ratio for the owner is about 22%, versus about 70% for HQ. Every 'AI ordering recommendation' is optimized for the wrong party's payoff. Nobody built the owner's-side calculator because owners fear retaliation and VCs assume HQ systems are neutral.
first_30_days: Use my three stores as the lab. Photograph two weeks of disposal sheets and hourly sales, then back-test the newsvendor plus markdown model against what actually happened. Build a LINE bot with photo OCR and a spreadsheet engine. Recruit 10 owners from union chat groups and Facebook franchisee groups. Run a free 4-week gain-share pilot with a signed baseline for each store. Publish a one-page 'royalty asymmetry' explainer that spreads owner-to-owner. Convert the pilot to paid at week 5.

title: Credit Ratings and Insurance for Virtual Power Plants
one_liner: A neutral firmness rating plus a parametric shortfall policy, so hyperscalers and utilities can buy VPP megawatts they can actually count.
customer: VPP operators and installers (pay for the rating), hyperscalers and utilities buying capacity (subscribe to reports), and reinsurers and MGAs (take the risk and pay a fronting fee).
problem: Sunrun, Tesla and Renew Home announced 16.8 GW of 'capacity-as-a-service' for data centers with no disclosed pricing, metering or verification standard. A 580 MW dispatch from 140k batteries on Sept 9 proves the tech works, but one event is not firm capacity. Buyers under bring-your-own-capacity rules need MW they can legally rely on.
solution: Publish a methodology that works like ELCC for distributed fleets: fleet-level P50/P90 availability by season and hour from attested device telemetry, with letter-grade tiers. Add a parametric policy, underwritten by a partner MGA or reinsurer, that pays the buyer if delivered MW falls below rated MW in a dispatch event. Start with public data from the ERCOT ADER pilot and California's DSGS program.
why_now: Hyperscaler-VPP deals, PJM's curtailment-or-bring-capacity rule and real dispatch events like Sept 9 mean there is finally enough event data to rate fleets.
revenue_model: $50-250k a year per fleet rated, subscriptions from buyers, and a fee or premium share on the insurance wrap.
non_obvious_insight: The VPP industry thinks its hard problem is enrollment. The buyer's hard problem is trust. Hyperscalers only pay for 'firm' if a third party is on the hook. Ratings plus insurance turn dispatch volatility into a financial product, and the standard-setter collects a toll on every MW sold.
first_30_days: Publish an unsolicited scorecard of public ERCOT ADER and California DSGS dispatch performance. Offer 15 VPP operators a free confidential rating in exchange for telemetry. Sound out two MGAs or reinsurers on parametric structure. Pre-sell a rating to one aggregator that is already pitching hyperscalers.

title: Heat-Number Vault for Water-Project Compliance
one_liner: A registry that matches mill test reports to heat numbers for every pipe, valve and hydrant, producing audit-ready domestic-origin binders for SRF water projects and tariff-tier evidence for importers.
customer: Consulting engineers, contractors and waterworks distributors on state revolving fund (SRF) projects, at $1.5-4k per project. Foundries and importers claiming the 10% US-melt duty tier are the second buyer.
problem: SRF-funded water projects need domestic-origin documentation (American Iron and Steel, Build America Buy America). Section 232 duties now hinge on melt-and-pour or smelt-and-cast origin, and CBP is auditing origin. Certificates are PDFs that do not match heat numbers, and reviewers reject packages. Small engineering firms have no tooling.
solution: OCR and match mill test reports to heat numbers and purchase orders. Flag gaps before submittal, generate the compliance binder, and keep a verified-origin record that can be reused for customs and loan disbursement. Add manufacturer-side badges for foundries with clean records.
why_now: Full-customs-value 232 duties began Apr 2026, with 10% for US-melted metal. EPA announced $7.2B in FY2026 SRF funds, and USMCA rules of origin are tightening after the Jul 2026 non-renewal.
revenue_model: Per-project compliance fee ($1.5-4k), subscription for distributors, and a verification fee for foundries.
non_obvious_insight: Water utility procurement already forces the domestic-origin audit trail that tariff and reshoring tools lack, and the same data proves duty tiers. One dataset serves both the reshoring and water markets, and nobody has connected them.
first_30_days: Pitch five small-town engineering firms and two waterworks distributors. Do three projects by hand with a template plus OCR at $1.5k each. Use the misses and rejections to design the matching logic.

title: Babel Tables for Multilingual Community Programs
one_liner: A tabletop translation hub that lets a senior-center lunch, ESL class or church group hold one conversation across four languages in real time.
customer: Senior centers, Area Agencies on Aging, libraries, faith groups and community colleges in multilingual cities, paying $150-300 a month per site plus hardware, funded from language-access and aging-services budgets.
problem: More than 25 million Americans have limited English proficiency, and isolated immigrant elders sit in language-siloed programs or nowhere. Interpreters cost $60-120 an hour, so programming stays segregated by language, blocking intergenerational and cross-cultural ties. Asian adults were the only Pew group net positive on chatbots for loneliness (37% help, 25% hurt), which signals openness to tech-mediated connection.
solution: A 4-microphone puck plus tablet that separates speakers and streams speech-to-speech translation to earbuds or phones, and captions on a table screen, for up to four languages at once. 'Table mode' runs low-stakes conversation card games, 'host mode' supports classes. Audio is processed ephemerally, with a human interpreter fallback for high-stakes moments.
why_now: Speech-to-speech translation reached conversational latency and usable quality in 2025 (translation in earbuds and meeting platforms), and small on-device models make private processing possible. State and city language-access mandates persist. Loneliness is a WHO-measured metric.
revenue_model: Hardware plus per-site SaaS, per-language add-ons, and contracts with city aging departments and Area Agencies on Aging.
non_obvious_insight: Translation tech was sold as an accommodation for one person and one interpreter. The bigger use is mixing: making the group itself multilingual so a Cantonese widow, a Spanish-speaking teen volunteer and an English-speaking regular can share one table. The unit of value is the table, not the user.
first_30_days: Prototype with a $200 speakerphone and a phone app. Pilot 'Table Tuesdays' in two senior centers (Chinese, Spanish, English) through a city aging department. Collect participation data over four weeks and charge $99 a month.

title: Investor-Cap Look-Through Checks for Title Companies
one_liner: An API that traces a buyer's LLC web to its parent and counts the homes it controls, so title and escrow can clear the ROAD Act's 350-home limit at closing.
customer: Title and escrow companies, closing attorneys and lenders in single-family-heavy metros. Secondary: mid-size investors (100-349 homes) who need to stay under the cap and prove it.
problem: The ROAD Act bars investors with more than 350 homes from buying existing houses. Compliance depends on affiliate holdings scattered across thousands of LLCs, which the closing agent cannot see. Large buyers will restructure into fragments, and mid-size investors suddenly need to manage headroom. Who is liable when a closing clears wrongly is unresolved.
solution: Entity resolution across county deed records, Secretary of State filings, registered-agent and address graphs and mailing addresses. It returns a portfolio count with a confidence score in seconds, an audit-ready evidence file for the closing, and a headroom dashboard for investors near the cap. Verify statute text, effective date, affiliate definition and exemptions first.
why_now: The law took effect in July 2026, and implementation questions are open now. Title agents are the natural chokepoint, as they already collect ownership details on entity purchases. Entity-resolution tooling and cheaper county record access make a small-team build feasible.
revenue_model: $15-40 per buyer-entity check. $500-2,000 per month SaaS for investors. Enterprise licenses to title underwriters.
non_obvious_insight: The people obligated to comply cannot compute the answer, and the people who can compute it are not in the transaction. The closing desk becomes the enforcement point, and mid-size investors treat their 350th home as a scarce budget, creating a second buyer for the same data.
first_30_days: Build for three metros where large single-family operators concentrate. Ingest deed and Secretary of State data. Sell paid pilots to 5 title agencies and 2 underwriters. Publish a free entity-count explainer to attract inbound.

title: Retraining-Backed Severance for AI Layoffs
one_liner: Employers replace resume-coaching outplacement with prepaid seats in shortage-role training plus a guaranteed interview pipeline, priced per re-employed worker.
customer: HR and people-ops leaders at 500-20,000 person employers doing AI-related restructuring; hiring employers in healthcare and trades pay placement fees.
problem: Employment of 22-25 year-olds in AI-exposed jobs is 19% below trend and recent grads are 42% underemployed. About half the earnings loss comes from landing in restaurants and retail. Traditional outplacement coaches people back toward the same shrinking roles.
solution: Displaced workers choose from vetted 8-16 week programs into shortage jobs (medical assistant, EMT, CDL, electrician pre-apprenticeship, revenue-cycle, dental support). The employer funds tuition and a stipend from severance budget. Hiring partners guarantee interviews. Use Workforce Pell where a program is approved. Success fee at 90-day retention.
why_now: AI-linked layoffs are drawing PR and political pressure. Workforce Pell has only 5 approved programs, so employer-funded pathways are the fast lane. Employers in experience-rated unemployment-insurance states may also gain from faster re-employment (verify by state).
revenue_model: $4-9k per participant paid by the employer, replacing a $3-5k outplacement fee, plus $1-3k placement fees from hiring partners.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders assume laid-off white-collar workers should look for adjacent white-collar roles. Those roles are the ones disappearing. Severance is already budgeted money, so converting a slice into a retraining voucher aimed at shortage roles costs the employer little and buys reputation.
first_30_days: Build 3 vetted pathways with local providers in one metro. Pitch 20 HR heads at companies that recently announced cuts. Run a single 25-person pilot and collect 90-day placement outcomes for references.

title: Guaranteed Midday Walker as Apartment Amenity
one_liner: Sell apartment operators a fixed on-site walker window as a renewal and lease-up amenity, with residents paying a discounted per-walk fee and the building paying a retainer.
customer: Owners and property managers of 150 to 500 unit multifamily buildings in dense metros, paying a monthly retainer. Residents are the secondary payers.
problem: A solo walker loses 35 to 45 percent of the paid day to driving between homes, parking, and building lobbies. Buildings, meanwhile, pay quietly for dogs: barking and noise complaints, damage from anxious dogs, waste on the property, and hidden-dog lease violations. Pet owners renew at higher rates than other tenants, but it is hard to monetize them with pet rent, especially where fees are capped or scrutinized.
solution: A walker holds fixed weekday windows (for example 11am to 2pm and 5 to 7pm) in the building, using the fob and package room. Residents book by QR code or text, and the walker walks compatible dogs from nearby floors in groups of 3 to 4 (dog compatibility is something a walker learns quickly), with a lobby handoff. Yield per hour roughly doubles or triples versus door-to-door, so residents pay about $12 to $15 per walk instead of $25 to $30. The building gets a monthly report on walks completed, incidents, and waste-bag use, plus marketing copy ('guaranteed midday walk') for lease-up and renewals. I could not confirm in this session whether a comparable product already operates at scale, so check competitors first.
why_now: Return-to-office mandates put more dogs alone midday. Big multifamily supply waves in many metros mean operators compete on concessions and retention, and are shifting amenity spend from gyms to services. Pet-fee restrictions in some states and cities push operators to bundle services instead of charging rent. Simple text-and-QR booking removes the back-office cost that used to make this unprofitable.
revenue_model: Building retainer of roughly $1,500 to $3,000 a month for guaranteed windows, plus resident per-walk fees of $12 to $15, plus optional add-ons (waste station servicing, dog-friendly move-in tours). Expand by selling to regional operators as a portfolio amenity program.
non_obvious_insight: The walker's real margin killer is geography, not demand. A walker's hourly income is decided by drive time and cancellations, so the fix is to put demand where the walker already is. What operators really buy is not walks, it is fewer noise complaints and higher pet-owner renewals, so price it against retention, not against Rover.
first_30_days: Start with a building where you already walk two or three dogs. Ask those residents to introduce you to the community manager. Pitch a 60-day pilot at about $750 a month with walk windows and a resident-sign-up QR poster. Measure sign-ups and complaints, then take the numbers to two more buildings in the same operator or neighborhood.

title: Power Passport: Scoring Dead Factories on Amps, Permits
one_liner: A database and paid inspection report that rates shuttered Midwest plants on the things reshoring manufacturers actually need (utility service, slab, crane, transferable air and discharge permits) instead of square footage.
customer: Reshoring manufacturers and their site-selection consultants (first buyer). Industrial listing brokers and sellers of dead factories (they pay to differentiate their listings). Regional economic-development bodies and utility economic-development teams (annual license).
problem: Brokers list buildings by square feet, clear height and dock doors. A reshoring plant needs enough energized 480V/13.2kV capacity, a slab that can carry presses and large CNCs, crane rails, and a transferable Ohio EPA air permit for a paint or wash line. Greenfield permitting and long-lead transformers and switchgear can add 9-18 months before the first good part. Meanwhile data-center developers are hunting the same brownfield shells for their existing utility service, so the buildings that suit manufacturing are disappearing without either side understanding what was in them.
solution: Build a parcel-level dataset of pre-2005 industrial buildings across Ohio, Pennsylvania, Michigan and Indiana by combining public air and wastewater permit records, county parcel data, utility maps, aerial imagery for crane bays and rail spurs, and Phase I history. Score each building on power, permits, structure and contamination risk. Sell a 'Power Passport': a 12-page report with a licensed industrial electrician's walk-through, gear nameplate photos, permit transferability notes and utility will-serve context, delivered in 5 days.
why_now: The 2026 reshoring wave and the data-center land grab are competing for the same shells. Transformer and switchgear lead times are still measured in many months to years. The gap between what manufacturers need and what listings say is at its widest, and brokers have no tooling to fill it.
revenue_model: $1.5k-$3.5k per Passport (paid by the broker or seller, or by the buyer). A 0.5%-1% success fee on closed industrial deals. $25k-$60k per year data licences to economic-development agencies, utilities and site-selection firms. Later, a capital vehicle that buys the best shells and subdivides them into permitted multi-tenant 'factory condos'.
non_obvious_insight: In a dead Ohio plant the building is the cheapest part. The energized service, the paper permits and the crane rails are the asset, and they are invisible to anyone who has not tried to open a factory. Every reshorer I know lost most of a year to power and permits, not to hiring.
first_30_days: Pick one metro (Akron/Canton or the Mahoning Valley). Pull public Ohio EPA permit records and county parcel data to list 150 candidate buildings. Hire an electrician for 20 walk-throughs at about $150 per hour. Cold-call 25 industrial listing brokers offering a free first Passport in exchange for a testimonial and a right to the data. Convert 3-5 into paying $1.5k reports and one economic-development office into a pilot licence.

title: Small-Claims Autopilot for Unpaid Invoices
one_liner: Take a solo operator from unpaid invoice to demand letter, filing, service, hearing prep and enforcement in a self-help flow.
customer: Freelancers, contractors and small B2B suppliers with $1k-20k unpaid invoices and no lawyer.
problem: Chasing fails, lawyers cost more than the claim, and small-claims procedure (forms, service, evidence, hearing, enforcement) is confusing, so most owners write off the debt. Cash is tight: nonemployers are less likely to be profitable and lean on personal funds.
solution: Connect invoices, email and texts. The system builds an evidence timeline, verifies the debtor entity and registered agent through state records, drafts a statutory-interest demand letter, files via e-filing where supported, schedules service, and prepares a hearing script and enforcement steps (garnishment and lien templates). It runs as a self-help tool, with a partner attorney for contested cases.
why_now: LLMs read messy invoice and message threads, e-filing is expanding in many courts, and nonemployer cash flow is under stress.
revenue_model: $79 flat per claim plus 10-15% of amounts collected, or a subscription for repeat filers.
non_obvious_insight: The demand letter itself resolves a large share of cases, and enforcement of the judgment is where the value sits, so the product should cover the full path. The regulatory edge is self-help positioning and attorney partners (the FTC's DoNotPay order shows the limits; prior knowledge).
first_30_days: Pick two states with online filing and $10k-plus limits. Run 30 claims for freelancers and trades sourced from community groups, and publish recovery rates and time to payment.

title: Collective Anti-Piracy Desk for 3D-Print Miniature Creators
one_liner: A creator-owned enforcement collective that fingerprints STL/3D-print models, hunts leaks across Telegram, Discord and marketplaces, and uses EU Digital Services Act notice, trusted-flagger and appeal rights to make takedowns stick.
customer: Independent sculptors and small studios selling printable miniatures, terrain and tabletop models via Patreon, Kickstarter, MyMiniFactory, Cults3D and their own stores (tens of thousands worldwide, top creators earning six figures). Also indie designers of other collectible models (keyboard cases, cosplay props) and the hosting platforms that want a clean enforcement feed.
problem: Files leak within days of release, spread through Discord and Telegram, get resold on Etsy/eBay/Temu-style marketplaces and printed into physical minis. A solo creator faces hundreds of infringements a month, and one-by-one DMCA notices cost hours, are ignored or are countered by repeat offenders. Brand-protection vendors price for brands, not solo sculptors. The EU Digital Services Act gave structured levers (Art. 16 notice-and-action, Art. 17 statements of reasons, Art. 21 out-of-court dispute bodies, Art. 22 trusted-flagger priority) and put very large marketplaces such as Temu and AliExpress under Commission supervision, but nobody has packaged these levers for small creators.
solution: (1) Geometry-based mesh fingerprinting, robust to re-meshing, scaling, splitting and hollowing, plus image similarity for renders and prints, with crawlers for leak channels, marketplaces and cloud-drive links. (2) A case engine that files DMCA and DSA notices in correct legal form, tracks counter-notices and statements of reasons, and escalates repeat infringers to the platform's regulator complaint channels. (3) An EU-established entity built to apply for DSA trusted-flagger status; Art. 22 explicitly favors bodies that represent collective interests and are independent of platforms. (4) A 'legit copy' program that offers print farms and Etsy resellers a licensed route, so leaks become royalty income.
why_now: The printable-model economy on Patreon and 3D-printer adoption are at scale. The DSA has been fully applicable since Feb 2024 and the Commission's 2025 actions against Temu/AliExpress make regulator escalation credible (verify status). AI re-meshing and generative 3D tools make exact-hash detection obsolete. Pressure from IP owners like Games Workshop pushes hobbyists toward original designs, so creator-owned IP is growing.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of $29-149/month by catalog size. 10-20% share of licensed royalties recovered from converted resellers. Enterprise feed for hosting platforms that want a vetted trusted-flagger channel.
non_obvious_insight: Piracy at this scale is a coordination problem. Thirty thousand creators each losing $5-50k cannot afford lawyers, but as a collective with formal DSA status they generate volume and quality that platforms must prioritise. The realistic prize is converting pirates into licensees (print farms reselling legally), not just takedown counts.
first_30_days: Sign 10 mid-tier Patreon sculptors for a free 30-day leak report. Build the fingerprint and crawler MVP with open-source mesh-hashing plus CLIP embeddings. Send DMCA/DSA notices through a part-time attorney and measure takedown rates. Convert reports to $49/month subscriptions. Register the EU entity and start the trusted-flagger application with counsel.

title: Blank-and-Recipe Kits for Desktop UV Printer Owners
one_liner: A monthly kit of pre-cut blanks, matched jigs and pre-calibrated height maps for the roughly 23,000 desktop UV printers that crowdfunding put into homes, so owners can fill machines and sell without fixturing trial-and-error.
customer: Owners of eufyMake E1, Longer ePrint and HeyGears-class desktop UV printers: Etsy and craft-fair sellers, keycap and phone-case micro-brands, makerspaces. Payer is the printer owner running a side business.
problem: Owners paid $1,500-$2,700 for a machine but still need to source consistent blanks, build registration jigs, tune 2.5D height maps, and finish for durability. Files are sold ad hoc on Etsy, but the hard part is physical fixturing and repeatability, so machines sit idle.
solution: A subscription that ships 30-50 laser-cut or CNC blanks (acrylic coasters, aluminium tags, keycaps, phone-case shells), a laser-cut alignment jig sized to the printer's bed, and a bundled PNG plus height map plus 'recipe card' (curing, primer and clear-coat steps) tested on the E1 and Longer. Add wholesale blank packs for sellers who want to scale, plus a 'sell this next' trend drop based on Etsy search data.
why_now: eufyMake E1 became Kickstarter's most funded project ever ($46.76M, 17,822 backers), Longer added $4.2M (1,584 backers) and HeyGears G1 $17.4M (3,911 backers). Units delivered from late 2025 through 2026 mean roughly 23,000 new owners are hitting the practical limits of the hobby now, and Etsy already has listings for E1 jigs and height-map bundles.
revenue_model: $59/mo blank-and-recipe kit, $0.40-$1.20 per blank wholesale packs (55-65% gross margin), and $19 add-on jig files. Later, sell a validated-blank certification to printer makers.
non_obvious_insight: Files are already a commodity on Etsy (e.g. 'Full Honor Set' bundles with PNG, Height Map, Print Guide, and popular E1 jigs, https://www.etsy.com/market/uv_printer_file), and the printer makers fight over ink instead. Owners' real pain is physical: one review notes prints need protective finishing, flat prints take minutes but textured pieces close to an hour, and heavy users hit ink-expiry chips (about GBP 240 of dead ink after seven months, https://www.makerhacks.com/eufymake-e1-review/), which a GitHub project was created to work around (https://github.com/joggie/eufy-timewarp). The same review says the business is 'high margin, low volume' (a keychain costing 85p sells for GBP 10-15; a GBP 5-8 tumbler up to GBP 25). Sellers who scale need repeatable blanks and jigs more than another file, and a consumable-with-recipe product is sold to them, not to the vendor. Demand sizing: https://www.entrepreneur.com/business-news/3d-printer-breaks-kickstarter-record-raises-44m/493857 and https://www.gizmocrowd.com/top-crowdfunding-campaigns.
first_30_days: Buy one E1-class printer (or borrow from an owner) and produce 3 kit designs: acrylic keychain, aluminium tag, keycap. Sell 50 founding kits at $49 in the eufyMake users Facebook group and r/UVprinting. Share before/after photos and per-piece margin math. Use a local laser-cut shop for blanks and collect feedback to lock registration tolerances.

title: The True Acceptance Map for Rural Transfers
one_liner: Voice AI agents call every receiving psychiatric unit and specialty hospital each night to learn what they will actually accept, and rural ERs text a number to find out who will say yes.
customer: Critical access hospital EDs, state hospital associations and state rural health offices (paid with Rural Health Transformation Program funds), and state behavioral health authorities. Subscription per hospital or per state.
problem: A rural ER holding a suicidal 16-year-old, or a stroke, trauma or OB patient, may spend 3-8 hours making phone calls to place them. State bed registries say beds are open, but the real decision is made by a house supervisor at 2am applying unwritten rules: no IV drug history, no one-to-one sitter, no autism, no patients over 250 lb, no out-of-state Medicaid, no aggression, and no calls after 9pm without a physician-to-physician call. Every ER charge nurse keeps a battered binder or a phone note of who says yes to what and who to ask for. It lives in one head, and it goes out of date when a house supervisor changes.
solution: Use voice agents to call each facility's intake line on a schedule and extract structured, current answers: true open capacity by population, unwritten exclusions, insurance rules, the name and direct number of the person who decides, and the hours that person answers. Serve it back through a plain SMS interface. A nurse texts 'psych, 16yo, Medicaid, sitter needed, hx cutting' and gets a ranked call list with the exact script to use (the words that get an acceptance). Only facility rules are collected. No patient data is ever in the calls. Later, sell a receiving-side listing so facilities can pre-qualify referrals and get fewer dead-end calls.
why_now: Every state has now posted Rural Health Transformation Program funding opportunities (as of August 2026), and care coordination and access technology are core uses. Research on bed-tracking systems shows registries still leave clinicians phoning to check appropriateness, especially for aggressive, medically complex, autistic and dementia patients. Voice agents from 2025-26 can now hold a natural two-minute call with an intake nurse for a few cents. The workforce shortage means intake lines are answered by fewer people, which makes the tacit rules more valuable.
revenue_model: $300-600 per ER per month for SMS access. State-level licenses of $100-300k per year paid from RHTP or behavioral health funds. A second line is a receiving-facility listing at about $500 per month per facility. The proprietary asset is a data graph of real rules that no registry has.
non_obvious_insight: The valuable data is not bed counts, which are wrong within an hour. It is the tacit acceptance criteria and the identity of the human who decides, and it can only be learned by phone at night. That is why bed-registry vendors (built on hospital self-reporting) miss it. Facilities that discover their rules are being published accurately will cooperate, because a dead-end call costs them time too.
first_30_days: Pick one state or region. Type up the founder nurse's own binder, about 60-80 facilities, into a spreadsheet. Wire an off-the-shelf voice agent platform to call each facility nightly and write results to a table. Put an SMS bot in front of it with a Twilio number. Give it free to five ERs in the region and compare call counts and time to placement before and after. Bring the numbers to the state hospital association and the RHTP office.
